title: Norris pips Antonelli to top spot in Mexico City FP3
excerpt:
Lando Norris finished fastest in Free Practice 3 ahead of the Mexico City Grand Prix, the McLaren driver just beating Kimi Antonelli and Charles Leclerc to the top spot.

The Briton posted a 1m 17.600s in the final minutes at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez on Saturday, leaving him just 0.001s clear of Antonelli, with Leclerc just one-tenth back.

Once the light went green at the end of the pit lane at 1130 local time Ryo Hirakawa immediately headed out, the Japanese driver replacing Esteban Ocon at Haas for the remainder of the weekend.

The Toyota World Endurance Championship driver had driven in FP1 on Friday and circulated frequently during the final hour of practice to gather vital data and experience ahead of his F1 debut.

Gabriel Bortoleto was another driver to venture out early on, but the Audi man immediately suffered a power unit issue with smoke coming from the back of his car as the Brazilian returned to the pits and failed to set a time.

Home hero Sergio Perez also failed to set a lap, Cadillac deciding to make a precautionary PU change on the Mexican's car ahead of Qualifying.

Antonelli, who stands on the cusp of claiming his maiden drivers' title this weekend, moved to the top of the times approaching the 20-minute mark with a 1m 18.754s on the medium Pirelli tyre, soon lowering the benchmark down a further tenth.

Times continued to tumble approaching the halfway point, Lewis Hamilton posting a 1m 18.268s before Ferrari team mate Leclerc registered a 1m 18.185s and then 1m 18.152s.

It took until less than 20 minutes remained for the leading runners to switch to the soft tyre and focus on outright one-lap pace, George Russell the first to make an attempt and setting a 1m 18.107s, stating "Turn 12 is so bad, there is no rear end".

Norris became the first driver to dip below the 1m 18s barrier, the reigning World Champion setting a 1m 17.873s, before Antonelli went top with a 1m 17.601s, and although Norris improved by a fraction, he still remained more than one-tenth adrift of Antonelli.

Leclerc backed out of his first attempt with the soft tyre after suffering a wide moment during the middle of the lap, eventually jumping up to second with another attempt after a strong final sector.

Drivers continued to exceed the limits, Hamilton suffering a moment of oversteer on the exit of the final corner, while Max Verstappen ran deep at Turn 4.

Norris went fastest in the closing minutes with a 1m 17.600s, just 0.001s clear of Antonelli, which remained fastest at the chequered flag.

Oscar Piastri (McLaren) was fourth behind Leclerc, with Red Bull's Verstappen, Hamilton, Russell, Isack Hadjar (Red Bull) and the Racing Bulls of Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad completing the top-10.

Nico Hulkenberg (Audi) was P11, from the Alpines of Franco Colapinto and Pierre Gasly, Fernando Alonso (Aston Martin) and Ollie Bearman (Haas).

The order was completed by the Williams of Carlos Sainz and Alex Albon, Lance Stroll (Aston Martin), Hirakawa and the Cadillac of Valtteri Bottas.

title: Hirakawa to replace Ocon at Haas for Mexico City Grand Prix
excerpt:
Haas have confirmed that Ryo Hirakawa will replace Esteban Ocon for the remainder of the Mexico City Grand Prix.

Hirakawa – who has acted as a reserve driver for the squad since 2025 – participated in Free Practice 1 for the American outfit on Friday at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez before Ocon returned to action during the day’s second practice hour.

On Saturday morning, Haas announced that Hirakawa would take over driving duties for the rest of the weekend in Mexico.

A statement released by the team reads: “TGR Haas F1 Team reserve driver Ryo Hirakawa will replace Esteban Ocon for the remainder of the weekend’s Mexico City Grand Prix, Saturday 31 October – Sunday 1 November.

“Hirakawa (32), a two-time winner of the FIA World Endurance Championship (2022, 2023) and 24 Hours of Le Mans winner (2022) with Toyota GAZOO Racing, participated in FP1 at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez on Friday 30 October – his third free practice outing of the season driving the VF-26, finishing 15th overall.

“The Japanese driver will partner team mate Ollie Bearman through final practice and Qualifying on Saturday and Sunday’s 71-lap Grand Prix – Hirakawa’s Formula 1 race debut.

“No further statements will be made at this time.”

title: Mekies predicts ‘one-off’ Mexico order in wind tunnel update
excerpt:
Red Bull Team Principal Laurent Mekies believes the unique challenges of the Mexico City Grand Prix could shake up the competitive order, whilst also revealing when the team’s new wind tunnel is expected to become operational.

Speaking during Friday’s press conference following FP1 at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez, Mekies acknowledged that Mexico City’s high altitude presents an unusual challenge for teams, with power unit performance and cooling requirements potentially playing a significant role in the weekend’s competitive order.

With the circuit located more than 2km above sea level, the thinner air creates additional demands on power units and chassis, forcing teams to make compromises to ensure reliability.

“I think there have been no unforeseen issues so far related to the altitude,” Mekies explained when asked if elevation had made any significant impacts on Red Bull's power unit.

“In fairness, we did have a PU issue with Isack [Hadjar] this morning and lost a bit of track time. The guys did a very good job and managed to send him back on track, but that was not linked with altitude.”

The Frenchman suggested that the conditions could lead to a different competitive picture compared to previous rounds, although he admitted it was too early to establish whether Red Bull would benefit.

“Both in terms of PU for the altitude and with all the compromises we are all having to make on the cooling side, we expect that this race could be a one-off in terms of pecking order.

“We don’t really have an idea whether we will have an advantage or a deficit this weekend. Only time will tell. But there is a fair amount of lap time, both on the PU side and the chassis side, that is in the game this weekend.”

Mekies reiterated that teams will need to balance performance against reliability, with the true impact of those compromises unlikely to become clear until later on in the weekend.

“In many respects everybody will not be operating at the optimum this weekend – PU side for the altitude, chassis side for the temperature. We are all ready to make some compromises to make sure our car can survive and our PU can survive in these conditions.”

Verstappen reacts to Lawson FP2 incident in Mexico

Mekies provides update on new Red Bull wind tunnel

Looking further ahead, Mekies also provided a long awaited update on Red Bull’s new wind tunnel, which is expected to replace the team’s ageing facility in Bedford.

The new state-of-the-art facility, which is being developed at Red Bull’s Milton Keynes headquarters, is an important step in the team’s longer-term development plans.

Mekies confirmed that the facility is expected to become operational at some point during 2027, with its impact more likely to be felt during the latter stages of development of next year’s car and throughout 2028.

“As much as the wind tunnel we are using has ultimately been producing extraordinary results over the last few years, it is most likely the oldest one on the grid,” he explained.

“As a result, if you jump to a state-of-the-art facility, of course you expect a competitive advantage from there. It’s not going to come as soon as we switch everything on, but it’s certainly going to unlock potential and give the talented people we have in the aero department another way to express their ideas.”

Asked about the timeline, Mekies added: “It's not ready yet. It’s something that will come online sometime during next season. Is it the first quarter, second quarter or third quarter? We will see. But it will be based on how much time we need to complete the calibration work and get it online first. So, it will most likely be for the second half of the 2027 car and hopefully for most of the 2028 car.”

The update follows comments from Max Verstappen, who has previously highlighted the limitations of the current facility.

Speaking to Viaplay in September, the four-time World Champion joked about the age of the existing equipment, comparing it to a wind tunnel “that comes from World War II”, before adding: “Of course you hope that as a team you can make a step there as well.”

Whilst Mekies acknowledged that improvements would not arrive immediately, he remains confident that the upgraded facility will offer Red Bull a competitive advantage as the teams looks to strengthen its position in the coming seasons.

title: Alonso cautiously upbeat after strong Friday in Mexico
excerpt:
With its long straights Mexico City wasn’t expected to be a strong venue for Aston Martin, but a solid performance on Friday has given the Silverstone team and their power unit partner Honda some cause for optimism.

Fernando Alonso was P7 in FP1, and while the position was not necessarily representative given the raft of rookies in the field and the problems suffered by various drivers, the 1.229s margin to pacesetter Charles Leclerc was at least promising.

In FP2 Alonso slipped back to P12 in the overall classification, but he moved closer to the front on lap time with a margin of just 0.769 to Leclerc – a huge improvement given that earlier in the season the gap was measured in seconds.

The AMR26 was benchmarked as the seventh fastest car, and the conclusion has to be that the package has thus far coped well with the challenges created by the high altitude in Mexico City.

The downside was a difficult day for the other car, with Jak Crawford stopping on track in FP1 and Lance Stroll playing catch-up in FP2.

Alonso admitted that so far the performance has exceeded expectations.

“Probably yes,” he said, when asked the question. “I was very open-minded coming to the weekend because Mexico is such a unique place with altitude and things, that I thought maybe we have a good surprise.

“At the moment at least on my side of the garage, the car is working well. I think Lance's car has some issues that they need to check for tomorrow.

“But part of the normal challenges in Mexico, with altitude, turbo speed, temperature, brakes, all these kinds of things that are a little bit on the limit. Apart from that, there are no big concerns into tomorrow.”

Alonso downplayed the challenge of low downforce levels: “No big difference, to be honest. We were all worrying about the lack of downforce this year compared to previous events, but I think the car feels very similar to the last few years here. So it was not an extra challenge, I would say."

Aston Martin’s Pedro de la Rosa suggested that the car is working well in the track’s many slow corners.

“It's fair to say it's slightly better than expected,” he noted. “Especially because I think probably the fact that there's a lot of low-speed component in this track, Sector 1, [Turns] 1, 2, 3, and 4, 5, 6 are very slow speed.

“Then you have the last sector, which is only mainly low-speed corners, second or first gear corners, which I think just makes us look a bit stronger. But anyway, it's still a challenge. Mexico will always be a challenge on temperatures, on the engine, on the braking. So we just have to manage that as well.”

Asked if the track could play to the strengths of an experienced driver like Alonso, de la Rosa added: “I think that from a physical point of view, there's no issues. So you have a long straight to actually catch up. There's not a lot of G forces. Also, the downforce you generate is quite low, because of the air density.

How 10 F1 rookies got on during FP1 in Mexico City

“But I think the fact that you are driving a car with very little downforce makes experienced drivers adapt faster. Also the fact that we have now two different sectors regarding asphalt means the drivers have to adapt a bit. You can push more on the last sector because there's more grip than on the first sector, which is the old asphalt.”

De la Rosa suggested that it was a good day on the power unit side.

“On the turbo lag, we haven't had many complaints from the drivers, which is positive,” he said. “So I think that Honda has done a very good job on the turbo lag, and minimising that effect.

“It's always an underlying factor, especially in a circuit like this at 2,200 metres. But it is mostly that we will have to manage engine cooling, brake cooling at a place like this. I think it's an overriding factor, rather than the turbo lag.”

title: Verstappen and Lawson get grid drops after ‘clumsy’ clash
excerpt:
Red Bull’s Max Verstappen and Racing Bulls’ Liam Lawson have been given grid penalties by the stewards following their “unacceptable” and “clumsy” incident during second practice in Mexico.

The pair – having missed FP1 as rookies Ayumu Iwasa and Nikola Tsolov took over their cars – crossed paths in the early stages of FP2 when Verstappen made a move on Lawson into Turn 12.

Lawson tried to get back ahead at the following left-hand turn through the stadium section, with Verstappen bouncing over the kerb on the exit and rejoining alongside the New Zealander, causing damage to the Red Bull’s floor and Racing Bulls’ front wing.

A red flag was thrown to recover the debris, and both drivers picked up their practice programmes – Verstappen finishing P5 and Lawson P9.

After the session, the stewards reviewed video footage and data, as well as speaking to Verstappen and Lawson, before issuing individual one-place grid drops.

“On the approach to Turn 12, Car 3 [Verstappen] was on a preparation lap and Car 30 [Lawson] was on a cool down lap preparing for another push lap,” read the stewards’ decision document. “The drivers of both cars behaved in a manner that was considered unacceptable by the stewards particularly in view of the warning that had been given at the Team Managers meeting earlier this day.

“Both drivers admitted the moves were unnecessary and ‘clumsy’.

“Noting that there had been similar incidents this year of actions between drivers in Free Practice, the stewards have decided to escalate the penalty from that of a formal warning to a grid position penalty particularly in view of the warning that had been provided at the Team Managers meeting and consistent with other incidents involving contact between the cars in Free Practice in previous years.”

Speaking after FP2, Racing Bulls team boss Alan Permane had also used the word “unnecessary” to describe Verstappen and Lawson’s coming together.

“I think one word, just ‘unnecessary’ in a practice session; completely unnecessary, and I say that to both of them,” commented Permane, after Verstappen criticised Lawson for “not very smart behaviour”.

"I don’t know what Max has said, I haven’t heard anything, but I’m sure he’s got his opinion and I’m sure Liam has got his opinion. Mine is it’s just not needed, and they can both do better.”

Verstappen and Lawson were also given a penalty point apiece by the stewards.

title: What the teams said – Friday in Mexico City
excerpt:
The drivers and teams report back on all the action from Friday practice at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez ahead of the 2026 Mexico City Grand Prix.

Oct 31, 2026 2:37am UTC

Ferrari

Ferrari were the only team to run both full time drivers in FP1, and both had a decent session, looking quick on the hard and soft tyres. Charles Leclerc topped FP1 by a reasonable margin, with Lewis Hamilton a few places back after running a touch wide on his flying lap. Leclerc picked up where he left off in FP2, again going quickest despite locking up on his soft tyres and running wide at Turn 1 on his first attempt at a flying lap.

But Hamilton’s second session was not so smooth, as he was forced to park up trackside with a PU issue.

Charles Leclerc - FP1: 1:18.128, P1; FP2: 1:17.827, P1

"Overall, our performance looks quite alright but we still need to work on some of our limiting factors. It was quite tricky on track today, as the surface was slippery, so we will work on that to find some improvements for tomorrow."

Lewis Hamilton - FP1: 1:18.866, P4; FP2: 1:18.512, P11

"It wasn’t the most straightforward day for me, as I missed some running in FP1 and then had to stop early in FP2. Despite that, the car felt quick, so it was unfortunate that we had to stop before completing the long run. From a setup point of view, I don’t think we need to make too many changes, as the car is working well. We’ll investigate the issue tonight and do our best to be ready for tomorrow. I’m ready to make the most of what we have."

MEXICO CITY, MEXICO - OCTOBER 30: Lewis Hamilton of Great Britain and Scuderia Ferrari sits behind a marshal on a moped to return to the pit lane during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Mexico at Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez on October 30, 2026 in Mexico City, Mexico. (Photo by Manuel Velasquez - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

McLaren

Leonardo Fornaroli had an eventful session for McLaren when he took over Norris’ cockpit. He locked up more than once, went for a spot of lawn mowing and sounded a little confused on the radio, but by and large he kept the car in one piece. As for Oscar Piastri, he had a quiet opener and finished inside the top 10. Roll on FP2, and Lando Norris looked strong, pushing Leclerc and winding up just a tenth off the Ferrari man. That was despite a big lock-up on the mediums for the World Champion, rendering that compound useless for the long runs. Piastri struggled by comparison, but he did catch one big slide that had the crowd on the edge of their seats.

Lando Norris - FP2: 1:17930, P2

"Not a bad day on the timesheets at the end of Free Practice 2, but the car is still proving a challenge to drive. The pace is definitely there but the field is incredibly tight at the minute, so it will come down to execution in tomorrow’s Qualifying. Thank you to Leo for his support Free Practice 1, we’ve still got plenty to work on overnight as a team, but the foundations are definitely there for us to build on."

Oscar Piastri - FP1: 1:19.376, P8; FP2: 1:18.469, P10

"Mexico is always a challenge with the altitude, low downforce and very little grip, but today felt slightly better than I expected. Even with a scruffy lap on the Softs in Free Practice 2, the underlying pace looks competitive, and the track was improving quickly as we went. We learned a lot across the sessions and if I tidy up the areas on my lap I need to, I’m confident we can be further up the order tomorrow."

Leonardo Fornaroli - FP1: 1:20.235, P17

"It was really exciting to be back on track in FP1 with McLaren Mastercard, and I’m grateful to the team and to Lando for giving me the chance to drive the MCL40. It was my first time on this circuit, and it wasn’t easy to find the confidence straight away to get the front tyres up to the right temperature on a track surface that, especially at the start, offered very little grip. In fact, a lock-up at Turn 1 ruined my first lap on the Softs.

"I’m really happy to be part of this team and to be working closely with the engineers, always trying to provide clear feedback to help develop the car to its full potential. It’s very important for me to keep gaining experience in Formula 1 as I develop as a driver: I’m already looking forward to getting back on track next Friday at Interlagos!"

Randy Singh, Senior Director, Racing

"All in all, it was a very productive Friday. We devoted a significant portion of our early practice sessions to set-up experiments and evaluations, particularly to adapt the car to the specific challenges of high altitude. Leo did a fantastic job of supporting our test programme in the opening session, providing us with a solid foundation on which to fine-tune performance in the afternoon. Both Lando and Oscar completed their planned programmes, using all three tyre compounds and running with different fuel loads on a track which, as is traditional here, offers little grip on the first day.

"Based on what we’ve seen today, the level of competitiveness is exceptionally close, with the top four teams separated by very small gaps and the rest of the field closer together than usual. Managing power unit and brake temperatures will be crucial for the rest of the weekend, especially in race conditions when running in traffic. We’ve seen numerous front-wheel lockups across the field, but we know where we can gain further lap times and feel well prepared to tackle qualifying and Sunday’s race."

MEXICO CITY, MEXICO - OCTOBER 30: Lando Norris of Great Britain driving the (1) McLaren MCL40 Mercedes on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Mexico at Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez on October 30, 2026 in Mexico City, Mexico. (Photo by Clive Mason/Getty Images)

MEXICO CITY, MEXICO - OCTOBER 30: Oscar Piastri of Australia and McLaren prepares to drive in the garage during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Mexico at Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez on October 30, 2026 in Mexico City, Mexico. (Photo by Bryn Lennon - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

MEXICO CITY, MEXICO - OCTOBER 30: Leonardo Fornaroli of Italy driving the (67) McLaren MCL40 Mercedes on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Mexico at Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez on October 30, 2026 in Mexico City, Mexico. (Photo by Clive Mason/Getty Images)

Mercedes

Kimi Antonelli ran wide on one of his first laps out on track, but after that settled in and looked relatively quick in the opening session, as Fred Vesti kept him company in the top three in an accomplished showing. George Russell joined the fray in FP2, and went third fastest on his second push lap on the softs, showing he seems up for the fight here. That was a tenth faster than his team mate, with Mercedes having a very solid opening day in Mexico City.

Kimi Antonelli - FP1: 1:18.787, P2; FP2: 1:18.044, P4

"First of all, it was good to be back in the car and feeling healthy today. It was an interesting Friday here in Mexico; it's never easy to get a read on the car, particularly in FP1 when the track needs a lot of cleaning. We tried a few different things between the sessions to get the car balance in a better window, and it seems that we improved things for FP2.

"There are definitely more things we can improve going into tomorrow and we have some work to do overnight. Ferrari looked very quick, but we will focus on ourselves, see where we can find more performance and hopefully put ourselves in a good position for tomorrow."

George Russell - FP2: 1:17.933, P3

"Fred did a really good job in the car and set us up well for my hour of practice; it was good to get into a rhythm so quickly after sitting out FP1. Mexico is always a unique challenge because of the altitude and the low grip, and that feels even more pronounced this year. We've been running high levels of downforce at most circuits because of the way the cars operate on the straights, so coming here we don't have the same step up in downforce that we would normally have at this circuit. That makes the car particularly tricky to drive, and you also have the challenge of turbo lag at this altitude.

"It's incredibly tight out there and every bit of lap time is going to matter. Ferrari look the strongest at the moment, which is perhaps not a surprise given the characteristics of this circuit, but I think it could go any way by Q3 tomorrow. We need to maximise everything because the margins are going to be very small."

Fred Vesti - FP1: 1:18.861, P3

"My FP1 session today was really satisfying. We worked through our full programme, gained lots of valuable data both for this weekend and the longer term, and helped set up the rest of our day. Personally, I was also very happy with how I performed across the hour. I knew my soft tyre lap was a good one, but seeing P3 on the timing screens made me extremely happy. I've put a huge amount of work into this car with the team, going back to the start of its development two years ago, so to have the opportunity to drive it here in Mexico and put together a strong lap was very special.

"I'm very grateful for the trust the team has in me and for the opportunity to show what I can do. These sessions are important for all us rookies, so I am pleased to make the most of it today. I felt comfortable in the car, put together a good lap and was really pleased to finish P3. It was a great experience and one I really enjoyed."

Andrew Shovlin, Trackside Engineering Director

"It's been a solid first day in Mexico. Kimi and Fred both did a good job in FP1, particularly given how difficult the conditions can be here with the altitude and low grip. Fred completed the programme we had planned for him and did an excellent job to finish P3. That gave us useful information to carry into FP2 when George returned to the car.

"Mexico is the hardest track to prepare for as it's impossible to simulate all the effects of altitude. We use Friday to understand the various issues that we are facing and come up with an approach to managing those through qualifying and the race.

"From the power unit side, we seem to be in reasonable shape with good delivery of power out of the corners. The cooling for both brakes and power unit is always an issue here but we were able to do decent long runs on both cars and whilst we'd like a bit more margin, it seems like all teams are having to do some management.

"The field is tight and we wouldn't put ourselves at the front of the bunch from today's running. We're struggling with a lack of stability on entry that moves to apex understeer. The single lap issues are actually quite similar to the long run, which should make it a bit easier to progress, but it's clear we need to find a step if we want to be challenging for the front row."

MEXICO CITY, MEXICO - OCTOBER 30: Andrea Kimi Antonelli of Italy driving the (12) Mercedes AMG Petronas F1 Team W17 on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Mexico at Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez on October 30, 2026 in Mexico City, Mexico. (Photo by Mark Sutton - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

MEXICO CITY, MEXICO - OCTOBER 30: George Russell of Great Britain driving the (63) Mercedes AMG Petronas F1 Team W17 on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Mexico at Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez on October 30, 2026 in Mexico City, Mexico. (Photo by Ryan Pierse/Getty Images)

MEXICO CITY, MEXICO - OCTOBER 30: Frederik Vesti of Denmark driving the (72) Mercedes AMG Petronas F1 Team W17 on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Mexico at Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez on October 30, 2026 in Mexico City, Mexico. (Photo by Chris Graythen/Getty Images)

Red Bull

Max Verstappen sat out the first session for Iwasa, who had a good hour for Red Bull. Isack Hadjar had a more difficult time of it, complaining about his steering wheel not being on straight, and also issues with the brakes. In the second session, Hadjar made his way up through the field with less to complain about. But his team mate did not have a smooth time of it, instead making contact with Lawson as the two jostled for position. That left the Dutchman with a heavily damaged floor, meaning he set his fastest lap time in a car that was definitely lacking in some downforce. He was later handed a one-place grid penalty for the incident.

Max Verstappen - FP2: 1:18.138, P5

“Today was a tough session and we probably could have done a little bit better, but we weren’t too far off. It is a different kind of challenge here as the high altitude is always quite extreme. It is tricky with the grip and the sliding, but I think everyone else will be saying the same thing as it never feels great at this circuit. There is some fine tuning to do and we just need to find more pace in the car to make a real jump. We got a little bit of damage from the incident with Liam too. The Ferraris are looking quick in this session; this is a track where you need to have more low-speed performance so it should play into their strengths.”

Isack Hadjar - FP1: 1:19.545, P11; FP2: 1:18.237, P6

“FP1 was a tricky session for us with only a few push laps on the board, but we managed to sort the issue out quickly and get some long running at the end. We made some good set-up changes for FP2, which showed. I felt a lot more comfortable in the car and we were more competitive. There are a few things we need to tidy up, but the long run has seemed good so far. The day started a little rough for us but ended with some positives. I think we can be in the fight.”

Ayumu Iwasa - FP1: 1:19.113, P5

“It was great to be back out there. Going into an FP1 session, you don’t really care about the ranking or the lap time; you just need to focus on doing the job. It’s been a little while since I last drove the car at Monza, but I could really feel the differences since then. The car performed well in both low-speed and high-speed corners, which gave me the confidence to push to the limit. It also felt quick, which always makes it more fun to drive. We managed to get some clear feedback that we’ll take into the rest of the weekend, so it was a solid session for me.”

Pierre Wache, Technical Director

“Ayumu did a very good job in FP1, where we got plenty of testing done. On top of that, he showed impressive pace for a young driver. In FP2, the performance of Max’s car was clearly affected by some damage, which we will be able to fix for FP3, whereas Isack’s session was solid overall. Still, we have a lot of work to do. The long run was more or less there, but we have performance to find, as the drivers are not yet happy with the balance. We are confident we can improve that with the set-up for tomorrow."

(Photo by Bryn Lennon - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

Racing Bulls

Nikola Tsolov was making his FP1 debut for Racing Bulls, and as a result his times were some of the most eye-catching. He wound up just two places and one tenth behind his team mate, Lindblad just scraping into the top 10 ahead of him. Arvid Lindblad had another good session in the afternoon, again finishing in the top 10. Liam Lawson’s FP2 will be remembered for some wheel-to-wheel action with Verstappen though, the two former team mates both winding up with car damage after fighting over the same piece of tarmac. Both were handed a penalty by the stewards for the moment.

Arvid Lindblad - FP1: 1:19.478, P10; FP2: 1:18.389, P7 Liam Lawson - FP2: 1:18.455, P9 Nikola Tsolov – FP1: 1:19.604, P12

Lindblad said

“Today was pretty decent overall. The altitude makes this circuit quite unique so FP1 was a little challenging, particularly as these are new conditions for the PU. The team made some good changes heading into FP2, and the car felt more alive. There are still a few things to work on ahead of tomorrow, but I think we’re in a good place. I really enjoy driving this track and I’m looking forward to the rest of the weekend. We’ll see what we can achieve in Qualifying tomorrow, but the target is definitely Q3.”

Tsolov said

“It was a super special day today and something I’ve dreamt of since I started racing. The atmosphere in F1 is very different, it’s crazy. I came into the session without putting too much pressure on myself and the team really helped me with that in making sure I felt the best I could, so I’m really grateful for that. The car is certainly different to what I’ve ever driven, it was tough to get used to but I got up to pace pretty quickly. I ticked all the boxes for what we needed to get out of the session and I’m looking forward to improving at every chance I get. I really enjoyed myself and I’m looking forward to spending the rest of the weekend with the team and learning as much as I can.”

Alan Permane, Team Principal said

“A strong day for us. The car has worked well across both sessions. Nikola did a great job for his first time in this car and at this track; the pace was there and he did everything we asked of him. We did a bit of aero testing with him and one of his objectives was to help with feedback and pick up differences in a couple of the specifications we ran, and he did that very well.

The car was in a decent window in FP2, the pace looks good on both long and short runs. Liam had an unfortunate and unnecessary incident with Max , which I think they both could have handled better. When you’re going for an out lap, it’s really important you do the last sector fast, which they were both going for.”

MEXICO CITY, MEXICO - OCTOBER 30: Nikola Tsolov of Bulgaria and Visa Cash App Racing Bulls and Peter Bayer, CEO of Visa Cash App Racing Bulls in the garage during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Mexico at Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez on October 30, 2026 in Mexico City, Mexico. (Photo by Rudy Carezzevoli/Getty Images)

Alpine

Pierre Gasly had a good opening session with a top six finish for Alpine, albeit with plenty of big name drivers sitting out. He was joined by Gabriele Mini, who was another making his FP1 debut. The Italian did well, although he did run over the grass at one point. In the second session, Gasly showed his FP1 result was no fluke with another strong lap to land solidly in the top 10. Franco Colapinto struggled to get up to speed after missing that first session, so he will be playing catch up tomorrow.

Pierre Gasly - FP1: 1:19.210, P6; FP2: 1:18.407, P8

“It has been a positively surprising Friday for us where we have had one of our better Practice days of the season so far. We arrived here expecting some challenges given the conditions and some uncertainties as to how the car would behave at this circuit. We have had two good sessions today where I have felt good right from the first laps of the day. The altitude here always makes the car feel strange but, compared to recent years at this track, I am feeling much more at ease. We have a good baseline to work from going into the rest of the weekend where we have a few areas to fine tune. It's not massive things which we need to improve, a bit on braking as well as getting the car more comfortable with some bumps in the high-speed, but it's quite small details. The gaps are also small, only a few hundredths between a few cars, and it will be about putting it all together when it counts.”

Franco Colapinto - FP2: 1:19.132, P16

“Even though it might not look that way from the lap times, the overall feeling after today was positive. We were catching up a little after missing Free Practice 1, but we are not as far off as maybe the timings show. I made a small error in the final sector and did not get the most out of my Soft tyre run. I know exactly where I need to improve for tomorrow and will also work with the team overnight to put ourselves in a stronger position. The long run pace was also positive, so if we can qualify well, we should hopefully be in contention for some points this weekend.”

Gabriele Mini - FP1: 1:19.946, P14

“That was an amazing experience for me to drive for the first time in an official Formula One session. Firstly, a big thank you to Flavio, Steve and the team for the opportunity, it was a truly memorable moment for me. As I left the garage, I was waiting in the pit lane with Lewis [Hamilton] in front of me, which was very cool. There were some legends of the sport out on track, people I have looked up to since I was a kid, so to be there with them was incredibly special. I would say the session itself was positive on our side. The team had a clear plan for me which meant some aero testing and data collection which will hopefully benefit the team in the future. I tried to stay consistent and build up the pace lap after lap. I did some good laps but if I am being critical of myself, I did not click everything together so that is something for me to look at and learn from. It's a very unique circuit with the conditions; tough on aero, tough on the power unit and there is a lot to understand and manage. That is all part of the learning process, though, and it was great to experience it all for the first time.”

Steve Nielsen, Managing Director

“Taking the day as a whole, I think we can be largely positive and confident heading into the rest of the weekend. We won't rest on our laurels though and we know we still have work to do and it's incredibly tight, particularly on one lap pace. Pierre really got into a good groove today and spoke very highly of his feeling inside the car, which is something we want to carry over into Qualifying tomorrow. Franco also fed back that he has a good feeling and knows where he can improve. The high fuel running in particular looked strong, but we know the field is more closely matched in Qualifying, so we need to look at extracting everything over a single lap. Also, it was a great job by Gabriele today, which was his first time in this car, and he did exactly what we expected of him.”

Haas

Ollie Bearman had an eventful end to his first session, pulling into the pits with a smoking car that initially looked to be caused by a brake fire. He was swift to jump out, but it turned out to be a PU issue and Haas needed to change that unit between sessions. Esteban Ocon had sat out the opening session, but he returned in FP2 and immediately complained about the power steering. He was not happy later on either, when he was told to switch to the mediums for his long run, not the softs. As for Bearman, his second session was also disrupted, as he briefly parked in a run-off area before getting going again. He wound up needing a software change to his car.

Esteban Ocon – FP2: 1:18.774, P13

“It’s always challenging when you miss out on a session, but Ryō did a good job and collected some valuable data. In FP2, we had a small issue at the start of the session, which we quickly fixed, and then it was about getting up to speed as quickly as we could. I still don’t feel super comfortable in the car, so there will be some adjustments to make and some work to be done overnight ahead of FP3 and Quali tomorrow.”

Oliver Bearman - FP1: 1:19.412, P9; FP2: 1:18.849, P14

“Overall, it’s been a positive day on track. We encountered a lot of issues in FP1, as we lost our latest spec engine, so we’re having to revert to the previous one which is a shame, as obviously there’s some performance involved in there. The car was a bit more tricky in FP2, so we need to understand why, but in general I’ve been happy with the day. I’m looking forward to tomorrow, I think things will be feeling better and I’m excited to see how it goes.”

Ryo Hirakawa - FP1: 1:19.982, P15

“First of all, a big thanks to the team. I’m really happy to feel the step in terms of performance since I drove in Budapest, so hats off to the team. We completed the run program, had no issues on the car, and we’ve made a step forward for FP2 with Esteban being back in the car. I’m really happy I had a good session, so hopefully we can score good points on Sunday.”

Ayao Komatsu, Team Principal

“We made a very good start. The car was competitive straight away, and both Ollie and Ryō looked very comfortable. It was good to hear from Ryō, as the last time he gave feedback was before our update, so he confirmed what our drivers have been saying about consistency, predictability, and stability of the package. Ollie was very happy, in low-speed he was mega, even in high-speed – which is one of our weaknesses – he was doing a very good job. Unfortunately, we had a PU issue, so Ollie’s FP1 was cut short at the end. The team did an unbelievable job between sessions to replace the engine and other damaged parts to send the car out on time. In FP2, Ollie was less happy with the car, operationally it was okay, but less of a clean session, if you like. Fundamentally, the car is still performing reasonably competitively, so we just need to clean up some areas overnight and prepare for FP3.”

Aston Martin

Jak Crawford did not have the best FP1, after he was told to park up trackside with an issue. That ended his running, Aston Martin later saying a suspected ERS problem had curtailed his session. Fernando Alonso though had a strong opener, finishing solidly in the top 10. The Spaniard impressed again in FP2, winding up 12th and showing the car does have some potential around this track.

Fernando Alonso - FP1: 1:19.357, P7; FP2: 1:18.596, P12

Lance Stroll - FP2: 1:19.631, P20

Jak Crawford - FP1: 1:20.803, P19

Alonso said:

"It has been a solid Friday in terms of performance here in Mexico, and we feel a little closer today than we have at previous events.

"It is always a challenging circuit, so it is encouraging to start the weekend on a positive note.

"The altitude brings its own difficulties, but we will keep working overnight and aim to get the most out of the car tomorrow and on Sunday."

Crawford said:

"It was a decent day for me despite an early end to the session. We had to stop the car on track due to a battery issue, but still managed to get some good running in today.

"Everything was going to plan up until that point so still useful mileage in a Formula One car for me and I enjoyed it.

"It was my first time in the car with the new engine so lots of things to learn compared to my last practice sessions and also to take away for my work in the sim.

"It felt quite low grip out there today and obviously we’re also trying to adapt to the conditions as much as possible to get the car in a good window."

Pedro de la Rosa, Team Ambassador said:

"Fernando looked quite competitive in both the sessions today. The car was working well in the low-speed corners, which maybe made us look a bit more competitive than usual.

"It was good to give Jak another opportunity in the car in FP1, but the battery issue cut short his session slightly. We need to investigate the issues with Lance's car because it was very difficult to drive.

"We will try and find solutions for tomorrow. As we see every year, cooling is a big challenge for all teams, and we need to keep an eye on temperatures across the weekend."

Audi

Nico Hulkenberg was one of the first to lock-up in FP1, locking both front tyres for good measure in what were tricky track conditions. But while that was less than ideal, what was even worse was the Audi team leaving a cooling fan on Freddie Slater’s car, and letting him complete a lap with it in situ. That led to a lengthy stay for the youngster in the pits as the team assessed the damage, and cost him some track time.

Gabriel Bortoleto regained his cockpit for FP2, but the team had found an issue with his car and he missed three quarters of the session as a result, only coming out very late on and thus goes into Saturday very much on the back foot.

Nico Hulkenberg - FP1: 1:19.608, P13; FP2: 1:19.023, P15

"It wasn't the most straightforward Friday for us. A few things didn't quite work as expected, and there are still some open questions we need to get to the bottom of. We've got a bit of homework to do overnight, but hopefully we can find some answers and be in better shape tomorrow."

Gabriel Bortoleto - FP2: 1:20.174, P22

“Not the easiest day for us. I sat FP1 out, as Freddie was in the car, but then we had a few issues before FP2 which meant I could not get much running in, completing only two laps right at the end of the session. Still, a big thank you to my mechanics for all the work they put in to get me back out on track for those final laps. It is a shame not to have had more time in the car today, but we will do our best to make up for it tomorrow in the last final practice session before Qualifying.”

Freddie Slater- FP1: 1:20.945, P21

“It was such a special day for me to finally get my first taste of the R26, and I am very grateful to the team for giving me this opportunity. It is something I have been dreaming about since I was four or five years old; overall, it was an incredible experience and one I will take a lot from.

“We stuck to our plan and ticked the boxes we needed to, which is part of the job when stepping in for FP1. Even though our running was slightly limited, I also took some good learnings from the session and got my first feel of the 2026 cars, which was pretty amazing. I cannot wait for Brazil now.”

Williams

Luke Browning and Carlos Sainz kept their sessions clean in FP1, although the latter was frustrated by traffic at one point. Work to do for Williams overnight, analysing that data if they want to make it out of Q1 tomorrow.

Alex Albon - FP2: 1:19.578, P19

"It was a better afternoon out there for me in FP2, with the car feeling more predictable during the session. We’ll take what we learned today and apply it overnight, hopefully taking a step in the right direction."

Carlos Sainz - FP1: 1:20.006, P16; FP2: 1:19.248, P17

"Overall it’s been a decent Friday. We changed some items between FP1 and FP2 which I could feel clearly in the car and they were a step in the right direction. We’re using these sessions as an opportunity to try some more experimental setups. Tonight we’ll evaluate what we can do with the car for the rest of the weekend and hope we can make some more steps forward for tomorrow."

Luke Browning - FP1: 1:20.869, P20

"It was great fun out there today - we did some good data gathering to bring back to Grove. It was a difficult session, as the resurfaced track was super dusty, but there were no major mistakes from my side. I’m just happy to have ticked off all my test items, including some good aero work giving the team more data to build on. It’s a great privilege to be trusted with all four of the team’s FP1 rookie sessions and to continue to be supported by Williams' Driver Academy. I’m looking forward to my next FP1 outing in Brazil next week, where I’ll continue to learn, develop and help push the team forward."

Cadillac

Sergio Perez exited the pits to huge applause in FP1 and had a clean session in front of his home fans alongside Colton Herta, who was driving in place of Valtteri Bottas. The Finn is being hit with grid penalties here after taking on a raft of new PU components to his Cadillac. In the second session, Bottas took his time getting up to speed and wound up just off his team mate’s pace.

Valtteri Bottas - FP1: FP2: 1:20.165, P21

“It was a tricky session, particularly coming into FP2 after missing FP1. The track is one I know pretty well, which helped me get back up to speed, but we’re still working to find the right setup and extract more performance from the car. We also need to keep an eye on reliability, particularly with the brakes and engine, so there’s still plenty of work to do ahead of tomorrow.”

Sergio Perez - FP1: 1:20.395, P18; FP2: 1:19.406, P18

“It’s a very special moment for me to be back on track at home in Mexico, in front of my fans and my people. It’s been a challenging day as I haven’t been feeling well, health-wise. Hopefully, I’ll be back to 100% tomorrow. I’ll focus on getting some rest tonight. It looks like we’re closer than we expected, which is positive. Hopefully, we can have a strong day tomorrow in qualifying and maximise our potential.”

Colton Herta – FP1: 1:21.365, P22

“Today was very enjoyable. I always have a grin whenever I drive this car. There’s always lots to learn driving a new track and with the challenges of the elevation which makes it tricky. But I had a lot of joy trying to figure that out and it’s great to have back-to-back weekends in the car. Every session you’re able to learn a little bit more about the car, about yourself and what you can do better for the next one.”

Marcin Budkowski, Team Principal

“Firstly, I am sorry for the fans who turned out to see Checo at the Fan Forum earlier today. Unfortunately, he was unwell overnight and we wanted to ensure he was fit enough to drive both sessions today in front of his home crowd.

"With a number of back-to-back races across continents, it has been a relentless schedule for the drivers and the team. We were pleased to see Valtteri back in the car this afternoon after another successful session for Colton as he built up more running in the car.

"On track, it has been a useful day gaining lots of data and learnings. This is a difficult circuit for cooling and the brakes, but the team have produced a good baseline on which to improve overnight. Our focus now is for both drivers to get a good sleep and come back ready for qualifying tomorrow.”

MEXICO CITY, MEXICO - OCTOBER 30: Valtteri Bottas of Finland driving the (77) Cadillac F1 Team MAC-26 Ferrari on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Mexico at Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez on October 30, 2026 in Mexico City, Mexico. (Photo by Clive Mason/Getty Images)

(Photo by Bryn Lennon - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

Pirelli

Simone Berra, Pirelli Chief Engineer

“Track conditions proved better than expected. Although grip levels were fairly low during the opening stages of FP1, the circuit evolved significantly from the outset, helped by the running of the support categories. As a result, the track offered better conditions than last year, as reflected by the particularly competitive lap times. In addition, the effects of aerodynamic load loss caused by the altitude appear to be less pronounced with the current generation of cars, which may help explain why lap times are so close to last season’s reference.

"During the first hour of running, most teams immediately chose the hardest compound both to familiarise themselves with the circuit and to help clean the track. Given that two sets of C3s could be considered surplus to requirements for the remainder of the weekend, this was also the natural choice for the cars entrusted to the young drivers. Both the Medium and Soft compounds performed very well, with a performance gap of around eight tenths of a second. On a circuit that naturally offers limited grip, the C5 was particularly effective in extracting its full potential.

"Data gathered from the long runs indicate a significant level of degradation for both of the softer compounds. This opens up several possible strategic scenarios for the race, ranging from a one-stop strategy, with more careful tyre management, to a two-stop approach. On the front-left tyre, we observed localised graining, which already showed signs of improvement between the two sessions. If track evolution continues at the same rate seen today, we expect this phenomenon to reduce further over the course of the weekend.”

title: How 10 F1 rookies got on during FP1 in Mexico City
excerpt:
Traditionally, the Mexico City Grand Prix sees a rush of rookies participating in FP1, with several drivers on the current grid having made their first public F1 appearances at the track in previous seasons.

This year brought a bumper crop of 10 youngsters running in Friday's opening session, with only Ferrari fielding both of their race drivers.

The group included some familiar faces, several of whom have participated in FP1 sessions across multiple seasons. Inevitably, the focus was on the three making their first public appearance in a current F1 car – particularly one driver who remains a genuine contender for a 2027 race seat.

Tsolov takes his chance

Racing Bulls boss Alan Permane made it clear a few weeks ago that F2 star Nikola Tsolov is in the frame alongside Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad. Inevitably, that added another layer of intrigue to the Bulgarian's public debut.

However, speaking to F1 TV, Permane stressed that the day was not a shootout.

"I said to him look, this isn't an audition, this isn't a rehearsal or anything like that,” Permane noted. “We know he's got pace, we know he's fast – we see that in F2. And I said to him what we're looking for is your feedback. We want to hear what you've got to say about the car. We want to hear about what you've got to say about the changes we make to the car, and then we want to hear how you are in the debrief.”

Having already gained some mileage in TPC running at Imola, Tsolov enjoyed a clean session and finished P12, just 0.126s shy of Lindblad.

“I think I was ready for it,” Tsolov said. “To be honest, I didn't really think about it too much, didn't really stress it, so I managed to arrive in a calm mental state.

“I don't have any reference. So, for me, it's just what it is. They've done already 20 rounds, so they kind of maybe felt different to the other places with the altitude, but definitely all the electric part of the car and the engine was something that I really had to get used to, and it's something very new for me.

“So, I think I can do a lot better – just keep on building onto that and learning more about how everything works.”

For Tsolov's F2 rival Gabriele Mini, Friday marked a first appearance in the Alpine A526 after TPC running in July. The Italian finished P14, with a best lap 0.756s slower than team mate Pierre Gasly.

“Both the team and I are pretty happy about how everything went,” Mini said. “We got a bit unlucky with the VSC timing at the end, which really didn't allow us to do any push laps on soft, just one.”

If Audi are proven to be correct regarding Freddie Slater, his appearance will be remembered as the F1 debut of a future talent. Not only did the Briton only turn 18 in July, but he has also yet to race an F2 car, so this was quite a step for him.

His session was ultimately blighted by issues beyond his control, with an error in the garage seeing him leave the pit lane with a cooling fan still attached and blocking a radiator inlet – an incident that later earned Audi a €7,500 fine.

Slater only got a brief unrepresentative run at the end of the session and had to settle for P21 with a best time more than 1.3s off Nico Hulkenberg’s best. Given his youth, he remained remarkably philosophical about the experience.

FP1 REPORT: Leclerc leads Antonelli in Mexico City as new faces make F1 debuts

"At the end of the day, it's motorsport, and that's how things go,” the F3 runner up said. “We're a team, and we win as a team, and we lose as a team. So of course, it was a bit frustrating, obviously, not to get many laps.

“But overall, that one lap that I did do was actually pretty good compared to relevant data. And a historic day for Audi to have their first junior driver in the car. It's a very special day, so we look at the positives.”

The young Briton gets another chance to showcase his talents with another practice appearance scheduled for Sao Paulo next week.

Vesti impresses with third

Of those with previous FP1 experience, the standout performer was Fred Vesti, making his third outing for Mercedes in Mexico City after appearances in 2023 and 2025.

The Dane finished the session in P3, just 0.074s shy of World Champion-elect Kimi Antonelli.

Vesti may be operating somewhat under the radar given that he has no obvious path to an F1 race seat. However, after the session he made the surprise revelation that he is chasing one and thus Friday was "perfect timing." The Brackley team certainly knows his value.

“Every time he gets in the car and does an FP1, he steps it up a level,” said Deputy Team Principal Bradley Lord. “And that was his most convincing FP1 so far.

“I think you can see that he's a guy who, away from this paddock, is racing regularly, obviously an IMSA champion as well, and is able to step in and ready to race at any point. So, a really good job.”

The only rookie to outpace his team mate was Red Bull’s Ayamu Iwasa in P5, six places and 0.432s ahead of Isack Hadjar. The comparison was skewed by power unit issues that compromised the Frenchman's session, but nevertheless it was a solid performance from the Super Formula star.

Having missed out on a 2027 Haas race seat, Iwasa’s countryman Ryo Hirakawa also had a good session as he logged P15, 0.570s shy of Ollie Bearman.

Mixed fortunes for the rest

Mexico was a third FP1 outing of the year for McLaren’s Leonardo Fornaroli following Barcelona and Budapest. It was a frustrating session for the Italian as he ran off track more than once, flat spotting his soft tyres in the process. The 2023 F3 and 2024 F2 champion ultimately finished P17.

“Overall, it was a tricky session,” Fornaroli said. “Of course, it was a new track for me, and it wasn't easy to build confidence. It was very low grip, especially at the start of the session, and then putting temperature into the tyres was very hard as well.

“I had a front lock up straight away into T1 because I didn't manage to put the right temperature into the front tyres, and this, of course, compromised the whole soft run and performance in general.”

Jak Crawford enjoyed his fourth FP1 run of 2026 with Aston Martin and he appeared to have inherited Lance Stroll’s luck with unreliability when he stopped on track with an ERS issue after running just 15 laps. title: Who is Haas F1 driver Ryo Hirakawa, the shock Esteban Ocon replacement?
excerpt:
Ryo Hirakawa is set to make his Formula 1 race debut at the Mexico City Grand Prix after Haas announced the Japanese driver would replace Esteban Ocon for the remainder of the weekend.

Haas has confirmed that reserve driver Ryo Hirakawa will replace Esteban Ocon for the remainder of the Mexico City Grand Prix weekend, handing the Japanese driver his long-awaited F1 race debut.

The 32-year-old will partner Oliver Bearman in final practice, qualifying and Sunday's race at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez.

Hirakawa is already familiar with the VF-26, having driven the car during Friday's opening practice session, finishing 15th before Ocon returned for FP2.

Haas has not provided a reason for the unexpected change, leaving questions surrounding Ocon's absence. However, the team did not confirm it is not because of illness.

Although Hirakawa has never started an F1 grand prix, he brings considerable experience from other categories, having won multiple world championship titles and the prestigious 24 Hours of Le Mans.

[Article continues below]

Who is Ryo Hirakawa?

Born in Hiroshima, Japan, on 7 March 1994, Hirakawa began his motorsport career in karting before progressing through the Japanese single-seater ranks.

He won the Japanese Formula 3 Championship in 2012, the same year he secured the Porsche Carrera Cup Japan title.

His performances helped him progress into Super Formula in 2013, where he established himself as a regular frontrunner.

Hirakawa enjoyed his strongest Super Formula campaign in 2020, finishing runner-up in the championship, and claimed four victories during his time in the series.

He also achieved success in Japan's Super GT championship, winning the GT500 title in 2017 with TOM'S.

However, his greatest achievements have come in international endurance racing.

In 2022, Hirakawa joined Toyota's leading World Endurance Championship programme, sharing the manufacturer's No. 8 car with former F1 drivers Sebastien Buemi and Brendon Hartley.

The trio won the 24 Hours of Le Mans that year before securing the World Endurance Championship drivers' title.

They successfully defended their championship in 2023, establishing Hirakawa as one of Toyota's most successful endurance racing drivers.

[Article continues below]

© XPB Images

How did Hirakawa become involved in F1?

Despite spending much of his career competing in Japan and endurance racing, Hirakawa has gained experience with several F1 teams.

He joined McLaren as a reserve driver in 2024, undertaking simulator and testing duties before making his official F1 practice debut at that year's Abu Dhabi Grand Prix.

Hirakawa subsequently joined Alpine as a test and reserve driver for 2025, taking part in opening practice at his home grand prix in Japan.

However, his association with the French manufacturer was short-lived.

In April 2025, he switched to Haas as the American outfit strengthened its technical relationship with Toyota.

The partnership provided Hirakawa with further opportunities to drive F1 machinery, including four practice appearances during the 2025 season.

He retained his reserve driver role for 2026 while continuing to compete for Toyota in the World Endurance Championship.

Hirakawa has participated in three FP1 sessions for Haas this season, including Friday's outing in Mexico City, providing him with experience of the current machinery ahead of his unexpected promotion.

[Article continues below]

Why is Hirakawa replacing Ocon?

Haas has not explained its decision to replace Ocon midway through the Mexico City Grand Prix weekend.

The Frenchman returned to the car for second practice on Friday, finishing 13th after Hirakawa had completed the opening session.

Ocon was involved in a tense radio exchange with race engineer Laura Mueller during FP2 over tyre strategy, although there is no confirmed connection between the exchange and Haas' subsequent decision.

The 30-year-old is already set to leave the team at the end of the season, with Ferrari junior Rafael Camara due to replace him in 2027.

Hirakawa's promotion comes against that backdrop, although Haas has only confirmed the change for the remainder of the Mexico City weekend.

For Hirakawa, the announcement presents an opportunity to make his first grand prix start after years of competing at the highest levels of Japanese and endurance racing.

At 32, he will become one of the oldest drivers to make his F1 debut in the modern era when he takes to the grid on Sunday, younger than only Andre Lotterer, who made his debut for Caterham at the Belgian Grand Prix in 2014.

title: MotoGP riders at risk of extraordinary ban over refusal to race in Qatar - report
excerpt:
MotoGP riders who refuse to travel to Qatar risk being barred from the final two rounds of the season, in Portugal and Valencia, according to a report.

Autosport writes that tensions between the grid and the championship's authorities have escalated sharply over the Lusail race, which remains on the calendar despite ongoing conflict in the Middle Eastern region.

Three-quarters of the grid voiced opposition to travelling to Doha during meetings at Phillip Island last weekend. But by Saturday's gathering in Malaysia, that number had supposidely dropped to just three riders, with most now resigned to making the trip.

Friday's meeting, held in Sepang, lasted an hour and had to take place in Yamaha's communications office after organisers rejected a request for a proper meeting room, a detail that underlines how strained relations have become.

Riders have been warned there is little room for manoeuvre. Most countries represented in the paddock are advising against travel to Qatar rather than issuing outright bans, meaning force majeure cannot currently be invoked to cancel the event without financial cost to the championship.

Organisers insist the race will go ahead as planned. Sources within the organisation say the Qatari government has given guarantees covering a paddock evacuation plan, financial protection against airspace closures and repatriation insurance in case of an escalation.

MGPSEG deputy managing director Carlos Ezpeleta visited Doha this week for a conference before flying to Malaysia on Friday, the same day riders held their meeting.

Unless riders can provide a clear, unequivocal justification for missing the event, they face financial penalties passed on by their teams, as well as possible sporting sanctions from the FIM stretching into next season, with any rider skipping Friday practice in Doha risking exclusion from the title run-in at the final two rounds.

title: How Ferrari's latest F1 engine upgrade is reaping the rewards in Mexico
excerpt:
How should Ferrari's strong performance during the first two practice sessions in Mexico, with Leclerc finishing first in both, be interpreted?

The ease with which the Monegasque's SF-26 managed the top positions was certainly surprising.

At the same time, it is worth pointing out that all the power units were being operated very conservatively on Friday in Mexico City.

This is primarily due to teams needing to assess the levels of heat exchange and stress on components such as the turbocharger that were actually being reached.

One significant detail, according to sources, concerns the fact that, for this weekend, where power unit operation is substantially different from that at any other race due to the effects of the lower air density, Ferrari has been able to establish specific operating modes that optimise both the internal combustion and electrical management parameters of the power unit.

However, further information suggests that this type of work only became possible following the introduction of ADUO 2 last September.

[Article continues below]

Treating the early pace with caution

The benefits of the upgrade have not translated into greater power, but rather into greater consistency from the internal combustion engine, enabling it to better support the different energy recovery and deployment strategies.

In short, ADUO 2 was not a tool for increasing internal combustion engine performance, but instead enabled more effective energy management.

According to sources, this has allowed the SF-26 to be more competitive at circuits with very different characteristics, including those that, on paper, are more challenging for Ferrari's power unit.

That said, ahead of qualifying and the race in Mexico, it is important to consider that power unit operating modes will be considerably more aggressive for a single qualifying lap than those seen so far.

Consequently, a deficit in Maranello's power unit that has remained hidden until now could become apparent.

However, it is equally true that both the race simulation and qualifying simulation have provided a useful basis for assessing the car's overall dynamic response and, above all, how it manages its tyres.

Indeed, the SF-26 has not only demonstrated an operating approach perfectly balanced with the characteristics of the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez, but has also been configured with a 'soft' setup from a dynamic perspective, prioritising traction.

This allows for precise tyre management, reducing thermal degradation, which is particularly characteristic of this circuit due to the low aerodynamic load imposed on the tyres.

In short, while Friday's results should be treated with caution, the overall picture is that the SF-26 and its power unit are extremely well positioned within their performance window.

In extreme conditions such as those in Mexico City, that is no small achievement.

title: Max Verstappen defended after Liam Lawson clash: 'I would have put him in the barrier'
excerpt:
Seven-time F1 grand prix winner Juan Pablo Montoya has stated he would have "put Liam Lawson in the barrier" if he were in Max Verstappen's shoes on Friday.

The duo collided during the second practice session as they ran side by side through the stadium section around the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez.

The incident did not go unpunished by the stewards, with both drivers now set to serve one-place grid penalties for Sunday's race.

While Montoya felt that Lawson had a right to stand up for himself when Verstappen attempted to overtake, he stated he would have been even more aggressive if he was in the Dutchman's car.

"I look at that and I understand that Liam felt that it was a late lunge, that it was a necessary late lunge, and he still made the corner," Montoya told F1 TV.

"And Max stayed there anyway, so he said, 'You're going to stay there, then I'm going to drive you off the track'.

"Liam went deep and used the whole track, then Max said, 'I'm going to cut the track and run over you'.

"You're not going to back off. If I'm sitting in Liam's position, I think what Liam did was the right thing.

"If I'm in Max's position, I would have put him in the tyre [barrier]."

[Article continues below]

Verstappen move 'unnecessary', says Hinchcliffe

As well as the grid penalties for both drivers, Verstappen and Lawson were both handed one penalty point on their super licences.

The clash has an added element of intrigue due to both drivers being part of the Red Bull set-up, and even being team-mates with one another a handful of races ago when Lawson was standing in for an injured Isack Hadjar.

Former IndyCar driver James Hinchcliffe insisted both drivers need to take blame, while acknowledging that Verstappen's escalation was "unnecessary".

"It's hard to say anything complimentary about either guy in this scenario," Hinchcliffe said.

"I imagine there's going to be quite a talking to back at the Red Bull at the end of all this because I think both drivers play a part here.

"Both drivers have some degree of fault, and ultimately you damage two race cars.

"Max had to do the rest of his session with a damaged floor. It's just sacrificing getting useful data.

"But clearly driving over the curb into what's essentially a team-mate is just so unnecessary. So both guys have to own a little bit of that."

title: Lewis Hamilton 'praying' after painful Ferrari issue during Mexico practice
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton's running during free practice on Friday in Mexico was cut short due to an engine issue.

Lewis Hamilton has stated he is "praying" there is nothing dramatically amiss with his Ferrari power unit after he was forced to stop on track during the second free practice session in Mexico.

Hamilton had just 13 laps under his belt before he pulled to the side of the track following an instruction from his team.

It cut short his preparation for the weekend, with team-mate Charles Leclerc going on to set the fastest lap of the session, as he did in the first practice outing.

Hamilton highlighted that the command to stop the car took him by surprise, as he felt nothing strange behind the wheel.

"I was feeling really good in the car, it's just my luck," Hamilton said.

"I think we did a really good job in getting the set-up in a better place. Just really unfortunate.

"I think we're really competitive this weekend as a team. I didn't get to do the long runs so I have no idea.

"I know it's really hard to overtake here, as you saw with some people out there. They're still investigating to find out what was wrong, and just praying that everything's okay."

title: Colton Herta takes ‘now or never’ F1 stance after super licence confusion
excerpt:
Colton Herta believes his chance to make it to F1 is in a "now or never" situation as he edges closer to finally obtaining his super licence.

There was some confusion on Friday of the Mexico City Grand Prix weekend as it initially appeared that Herta had earned the required 40th point for the licence after completing his 24th lap of FP1 as he deputised for Valtteri Bottas.

However, it emerged that Cadillac's own internal maths was wrong after an error on the IndyCar website had Herta down as sixth place in the 2025 standings, earning him two super licence points than the seventh place in the standings he had actually earned.

It all means that instead of having 40 points, Herta remains on 39, and is expected to get another practice outing in Brazil next time out to finally qualify for a potential F1 race seat, if Bottas is dropped.

The race for the second Cadillac seat is heating up, with Fred Vesti declaring an interest after a strong FP1 for Mercedes, but Herta, who is Cadillac's own internal driver, believes his long-held dream of making it to F1 is finally facing a reckoning.

"To be honest, I haven't paid too much attention. I was literally walking to go do the media stuff, and that was the first time I had heard about it," Herta told media, including RacingNews365, of the super licence confusion.

"Obviously, we were still doing our meetings and whatnot, so I didn't talk to anybody about it, and as far as I was concerned, going into the weekend, if I did 100km here, I would have 40 [points], so I'm not sure what's changed or why stuff has changed or if it even has, so I think I have to wait and see."

Turning to whether this was his last chance to make it as a full-time grand prix racer, Herta declared that it was.

"I think so, and as far as it being like now or never, I don't think I can go back to IndyCar and then have another chance in Formula 1," he said.

"Whether that means next year or the following year, I really don't know what the plan is at the moment, so I think we'll have to wait and see. I think some decisions hopefully will be made within the next month.

"For me, I think it would be great the sooner the better to know. Going into November, you want to know what you're doing next year. So for me, that's kind of like the main thing is just to know what I'm doing next year."

The Californian then added that he hoped Cadillac giving him the FP1 outings was heading towards his desired outcome.

"I hope so," he said when asked if he was a realistic candidate for the seat.

"Or else, I don't know why I'd be doing this. I think Cadillac have shown a lot of faith in me doing these FP1s - they've put a lot of resources behind me to get me ready to be in the Formula 1 seat.

"I hope that's reciprocated and I can make it, but right now, it's all guesses."

[Article continues below]

'Super licence monkey off my back'

Expanding further, Herta declared that he is "1,000% ready" to step into a race seat in F1 in 2027, if chosen.

"I think every time I get in the car, I feel more comfortable and I'm able to push a bit more," he said.

"I think once I get that super licence monkey off my back, then I can really kind of push everything as hard as I want.

"I back myself 100% on everything. I think I can be as quick as anybody. I think, and I think I have the capability of learning very quickly too, and picking up on things. So, 1,000%, I back myself in being able to do this."
